title: Episode 201: The Assyrian Empire: Sennacherib, the Angel of Death, and the Fall of Nineveh

In 701 BC, the invincible Assyrian army under Emperor Sennacherib surrounded the mountain fortress of Jerusalem, preparing to slaughter its inhabitants and erase the Kingdom of Judah from history. Anticipating the siege, King Hezekiah executed an astonishing engineering miracle, carving a seventeen-hundred-foot subterranean tunnel through solid bedrock to channel the Gihon Spring into the city. While Assyrian field commander Rabshakeh taunted the starving defenders on the walls in Hebrew, Prophet Isaiah issued a defiant prophecy: Sennacherib would not shoot a single arrow into the city. In a single night of biblical drama confirmed by ancient historian Herodotus, an invisible cataclysm struck the Assyrian camp, leaving one hundred and eighty-five thousand soldiers dead and forcing Sennacherib to flee in disgrace to Nineveh, where he was assassinated by his own sons. Discover the miracle of Jerusalem and the catastrophic collapse of Nineveh.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we conclude our Assyrian Empire series with one of the most dramatic sieges in world history. Surrounded by the undefeated forces of Nineveh, King Hezekiah and the Prophet Isaiah stood firm against psychological warfare, witnessing a supernatural deliverance that echoed through the centuries. Here is George with the story of Hezekiah's tunnel, the Angel of Death, and the burning of Nineveh.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: HEZEKIAH'S SUBTERRANEAN WATER TUNNEL
When King Hezekiah saw that Sennacherib was determined to besiege Jerusalem, he took counsel with his princes, military commanders, and engineering guilds. Jerusalem's primary strategic vulnerability was its water supply: the freshwater Gihon Spring was situated outside the fortified city walls in the Kidron Valley. If the Assyrians seized the spring, the city would perish of thirst within days, while providing abundant fresh water to the invading legions: 'Why should the kings of Assyria come, and find much water?' Hezekiah ordered the outside spring blocked from sight, concealing the cave entrance beneath heavy masonry, clay, and desert earth. Then, he launched one of the most astonishing civil engineering feats of antiquity: carving a subterranean aqueduct through seventeen hundred and fifty feet of solid limestone bedrock beneath the City of David. Working in complete darkness with iron picks, guided only by the flickering light of oil lamps, two teams of miners started at opposite ends—one at the Gihon Spring, the other at the Pool of Siloam inside the walls—digging toward each other along an S-shaped trajectory, navigating underground acoustic echoes and fracture lines. In 1880, a young boy wading in the tunnel discovered the famous Siloam Inscription carved into the rock wall, describing the breathless moment the two teams broke through: 'The miners struck pick against pick, and the water flowed from the spring to the pool for twelve hundred cubits, while the height of the rock above the heads of the miners was one hundred cubits.' Fresh spring water was secured inside Jerusalem's walls, providing unbroken life to a besieged mountain stronghold.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE TAUNTS OF THE RABSHAKEH
Sennacherib dispatched a massive military contingent from the bloody siege of Lachish to Jerusalem, commanded by his chief cupbearer and military propagandist, the Rabshakeh. Standing by the Conduit of the Upper Pool on the highway of the Fuller's Field, the Rabshakeh halted beneath the high battlements of Jerusalem. When Hezekiah's royal ministers—Eliakim the palace superintendent, Shebna the royal scribe, and Joah the recorder—begged him to speak in Aramaic, the international language of diplomacy, so that the common soldiers on the walls would not understand the terrifying threats, the Rabshakeh laughed contemptuously. Stepping forward, he shouted in loud, fluent Judean Hebrew directly to the terrified citizens lining the parapets. He ridiculed their trust in Egypt as a 'broken reed of a staff that pierces the hand of him who leans upon it,' and mocked their faith in God: 'Has any god of the nations ever delivered his land out of the hand of the king of Assyria? Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah? Have they delivered Samaria out of my hand?' He warned the citizens that Hezekiah was leading them to starve behind the walls until they would be forced to eat their own dung and drink their own urine. The Hebrew soldiers held their breath in disciplined silence, gripping their spears and obeying King Hezekiah's strict command: answer him not a single word.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: ISAIAH'S PROPHECY IN THE TEMPLE
When King Hezekiah heard the report of the Rabshakeh's blasphemous taunts, he tore his royal robes, covered himself in coarse sackcloth, and walked into the Temple of Solomon on Mount Moriah. Receiving a threatening, written ultimatum from Sennacherib demanding unconditional surrender, Hezekiah performed an act of profound spiritual vulnerability: he walked into the sanctuary, unrolled the parchment letter on the stone floor before the Ark of the Covenant, and knelt in fervent prayer: 'O Lord God of Israel, which dwellest between the cherubims, thou art the God, even thou alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth... Incline thine ear, O Lord, and hear; open thine eyes, and see: and hear the words of Sennacherib, which hath sent him to reproach the living God.' Moments later, an inspired message arrived from the court prophet Isaiah, son of Amoz. Isaiah delivered God's defiant answer to the emperor of Nineveh: 'The virgin, the daughter of Zion, hath despised thee, and laughed thee to scorn; the daughter of Jerusalem hath shaken her head at thee... Therefore thus saith the Lord concerning the king of Assyria: He shall not come into this city, nor shoot an arrow there, nor come before it with shield, nor cast a bank against it. By the way that he came, by the same shall he return, and shall not come into this city, saith the Lord. For I will defend this city, to save it, for mine own sake, and for my servant David's sake.' Faith stood resolute against imperial might.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE SMITTEN CAMP: 185,000 FALL IN THE NIGHT
That very night, an invisible cataclysm struck the Assyrian siege camp outside the walls of Jerusalem. The biblical Book of Kings and the Book of Isaiah record the staggering event in solemn, awe-inspiring prose: 'And it came to pass that night, that the angel of the Lord went out, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians an hundred fourscore and five thousand: and when they arose early in the morning, behold, they were all dead corpses.' One hundred and eighty-five thousand seasoned, iron-clad warriors died where they lay, their weapons dropping from lifeless hands into the dust. Ancient Greek historian Herodotus recorded an Egyptian version of the disaster, reporting that a plague of field mice swarmed the Assyrian camp in the night, gnawing through their bowstrings, quivers, and leather shield straps, leaving the army defenseless and decimated by a virulent outbreak of bubonic plague. Modern epidemiologists suggest a sudden, devastating epidemic swept through the crowded siege camp. At dawn, Judean sentinels looking out from the battlements saw thousands of motionless bodies lying under the morning mist. Regardless of the physical vector, Sennacherib was broken. Stunned by the catastrophic loss of his elite army, the proud emperor who had boasted of caging Hezekiah like a bird broke camp in the dead of night and fled in humiliated retreat back to Nineveh, never to set foot in the land of Judah again.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE ASSASSINATION OF SENNACHERIB: 681 BC
Back in his magnificent capital of Nineveh, Sennacherib ruled for twenty more years, building palaces, aqueducts, and gardens, yet haunted by the humiliation outside Jerusalem. His domestic court was a viper's pit of family jealousy and ambition. Sennacherib bypassed his older sons to designate his younger son, Esarhaddon, as the official heir to the throne. His older sons, Adrammelech and Sharezer, conspired in bitter fury. In January 681 BC, while the sixty-year-old emperor was bowing in humble worship inside the temple of his god Nisroch, his two sons stepped behind him with drawn daggers and struck him down, bathing the sacred altar in royal blood. The biblical Book of Kings and contemporary Babylonian cuneiform chronicles corroborate the patricide in exact detail. The royal palace was thrown into chaos as the assassins fled into the rugged mountains of Ararat in Armenia. Esarhaddon marched on Nineveh with loyal troops, crushing his brothers' factions in a brief civil war and claiming the throne, fulfilling the ancient warning that those who live by the sword shall perish by the sword.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: ASHURBANIPAL AND THE GREAT LIBRARY OF NINEVEH
Under Esarhaddon's son, Ashurbanipal—who ruled from 668 to 627 BC—the Assyrian Empire reached its absolute territorial zenith, marching into Egypt to sack the ancient pharaonic capital of Thebes. Ashurbanipal was a rare anomaly among Assyrian kings: he was not merely a brutal conqueror who boasted of putting dog collars on captured kings, but a deeply cultivated scholar who could read ancient Sumerian and Akkadian cuneiform inscriptions carved on stone from before the Great Flood. In his palace at Nineveh, Ashurbanipal established the greatest library of the ancient world. Dispatched scribes across Mesopotamia copied and confiscated every written text they could find: royal decrees, medical treatises, astronomical observations, mathematical calculations, and ancient literary epics. When British archaeologist Austen Henry Layard excavated Nineveh in the 1840s, he unearthed over thirty thousand clay cuneiform tablets from Ashurbanipal's library—including the immortal Epic of Gilgamesh with its ancient account of Utnapishtim's ark and the Deluge. It was the greatest archaeological treasure trove of ancient Mesopotamian civilization ever discovered, unlocking the secrets of humanity's earliest literature.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE BURNING OF NINEVEH: 612 BC
Yet the immense weight of Assyria's cruelty had sown the seeds of its own total destruction. Conquered nations nursed an unquenchable, burning hatred for the butchers of Nineveh. When Ashurbanipal died in 627 BC, a coalition of vengeance formed between the rising Chaldean Babylonians under Nabopolassar and the fierce mountain horsemen of the Medes under Cyaxares. In 612 BC, their combined armies surrounded the colossal walls of Nineveh. An unusually heavy spring flood on the Khosr River broke through a section of the city walls, allowing the Babylonian and Median warriors to pour through the breach. What followed was an apocalyptic orgy of destruction. Nineveh was looted, its magnificent palaces torched, and its citizens put to the sword. The heat of the conflagration was so intense that it baked Ashurbanipal's clay library tablets into indestructible ceramic, preserving them for modern archaeologists. The Hebrew prophet Nahum had prophesied the total annihilation of the bloodstained city: 'Nineveh is laid waste: who will bemoan her? All that hear the bruit of thee shall clap the hands over thee: for upon whom hath not thy wickedness passed continually?' Within two generations, the sand covered the ruins so completely that when Xenophon marched ten thousand Greek soldiers past the mounds two hundred years later, he did not even know that the greatest empire in the world lay buried beneath his boots.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The iron empire of Assyria vanished beneath the sands of Mesopotamia, leaving behind only clay tablets and the memory of its terrifying cruelty. But rising from its ashes was the golden, intellectual empire of the Chaldeans: Babylon. Next week, we begin our exploration of The Babylonian Empire with Episode 204: Nebuchadnezzar's Dream: the Ishtar Gate of gleaming lapis lazuli, the Hanging Gardens built for a homesick queen, the colossus of gold, the fiery furnace, and the prophet Daniel. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
